issues.legal_issue: A cultivating tenant whose qualifying occupation of agricultural land predated the estate’s takeover acquired entitlement to a ryotwari patta, and a later law cancelling subsisting institutional leases did not apply where no such lease subsisted.
material_facts: The land was within an estate notified and taken over under the estate-abolition law.
A final civil decree found that the occupant and his predecessors had cultivated and possessed the land as tenants before the notified date.
A separate suit seeking rent on the basis of an alleged later rent deed was dismissed, and that determination became final between the parties.
The alleged lease relationship was therefore not subsisting when the later endowments law commenced.
issues.conclusion: The occupant automatically became entitled to a ryotwari patta under Section 11 of the 1948 Act. Section 82 of the 1987 Act did not apply because he was not a holder of a subsisting lease of institutional agricultural land when that Act commenced.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 11 of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 provide for the transfer and vesting of the estate, termination of the landlord–ryot relationship, and entitlement of a qualifying ryot to a ryotwari patta. Section 82 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987 applies to a lease of institutional agricultural land subsisting at commencement of that Act. Muddada Chayanna v. Karnam Narayana, AIR 1979 SC 1320, concerned a different relationship between the parties and did not assist the institution here.

rule.if: agricultural_tenure_dispute and qualifying_ryot_before_takeover and prior_decree_confirmed_tenancy and not institutional_lease_subsisted_at_later_law_commencement

predicates.agricultural_tenure_dispute: The proceeding concerned the rights of an occupant and an institution in agricultural land following an estate takeover.
predicates.qualifying_ryot_before_takeover: The occupant or the occupant’s predecessors cultivated and possessed the land as tenants before the estate was taken over.
predicates.prior_decree_confirmed_tenancy: A final determination between the parties confirmed the occupant’s earlier tenancy and possession.
predicates.institutional_lease_subsisted_at_later_l: A lease of the institutional agricultural land remained in force when the later law commenced.

issues.definition: When an agricultural-tenure dispute involves a qualifying pre-takeover ryot whose tenancy was finally confirmed and no institutional lease remained in force at commencement of the later law, the later lease-cancellation rule does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A final civil-court decree determining possession and tenancy could not be disregarded on the ground that the civil court lacked jurisdiction where the statutory adjudication concerned revenue purposes.
material_facts: The civil court decreed the occupant’s suit and dismissed the institution’s rent claim.
The decrees determined the parties’ possession and rejected the alleged landlord–tenant relationship based on a later rent deed.
The decrees became final between the parties.
The institution later contended that the civil court lacked jurisdiction and that the decrees were therefore not binding.
issues.conclusion: The civil decrees were binding between the parties; the contention that the civil court lacked jurisdiction was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, (1985) 4 SCC 10, explains that statutory finality of decisions under the estate-abolition law does not, by itself, establish exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction; the scheme, subject matter, and adequacy of statutory remedies must be considered. It also explains that decisions concerning ryotwari pattas serve the Act’s revenue purposes and that a determination of the land’s nature or character may be incidental to that purpose. The Court relied on the principles stated in Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1968) 3 SCR 662.

rule.if: challenge_to_binding_civil_judgment and prior_civil_decree_final_between_parties and decree_decided_possession_or_tenancy and statutory_adjudication_served_revenue_purposes

predicates.challenge_to_binding_civil_judgment: A party to a dispute challenged whether a civil-court judgment could bind the parties because of an asserted lack of civil-court jurisdiction.
predicates.prior_civil_decree_final_between_parties: The earlier civil-court decree had become final between the parties.
predicates.decree_decided_possession_or_tenancy: The earlier decree determined the parties’ possession or their alleged landlord–tenant relationship.
predicates.statutory_adjudication_served_revenue_pu: The relevant statutory adjudication concerned revenue administration and recovery rather than conclusively determining rights for every purpose.

issues.definition: When a final civil decree between the parties decided possession or tenancy and the statutory adjudication serves revenue purposes, the decree remains binding between those parties.

issues.legal_issue: A possession-based claim is not time-barred by reference to the date of an earlier decree when the claim arose from a later threatened interference with possession.
material_facts: The occupant remained in possession of the land, and possession itself was not disputed.
The institution asserted that the occupant possessed the land as its tenant.
The occupant relied on a later alleged interference with possession as the event giving rise to the claim and pursued an execution application in response.
issues.conclusion: The claim was not barred by limitation; the relevant date was when possession was allegedly threatened, not the date of the earlier decree.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the alleged threat to possession as the relevant event for determining limitation and rejected using the date of the earlier decree as the starting point. No limitation provision or earlier case was identified for this conclusion.

predicates.limitation_challenge_to_possession_claim: The proceeding challenged whether a claim concerning possession was brought in time.
predicates.possession_continued: The claimant remained in possession, and the opposing party did not dispute that possession existed.
predicates.claim_arose_from_later_threat_to_possess: The claimant relied on a later alleged threat or interference with possession as the event giving rise to the claim.

issues.definition: When a possession-based claim arises from a later threat to continuing possession, the claim is not barred by limitation merely because an earlier decree was made earlier.
